pipeline.attack_summary: Attackers exploit CVE-2024-35250 in Microsoft Windows Kernel Streaming Service to achieve local privilege escalation through kernel-mode driver vulnerabilities. The attack leverages IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag to bypass security checks, enabling arbitrary kernel function calls and ultimately privilege escalation. Additionally, HiatusRAT targets IoT devices like web cameras and DVRs using CVEs including CVE-2017-7921, CVE-2018-9995, CVE-2020-25078, CVE-2021-33044, CVE-2021-36260 and weak passwords. A coordinated ransomware campaign involving DrayTek routers exploits zero-day vulnerabilities to gain initial access, harvest credentials, and deploy multiple ransomware families.

pipeline.attack_summary: Slingshot is a sophisticated APT that compromises Mikrotik routers via Winbox Loader, downloads malicious DLLs like ipv4.dll which acts as a downloader for other components. It uses kernel-mode modules such as Cahnadr/NDriver and user-mode GollumApp to achieve persistence, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration. The malware employs techniques including DLL hijacking, driver signature bypassing, encrypted file systems, and disabling defragmentation to evade detection.

rules_yaml:
title: GRIFFON Implant Initial Access via Macro-Executed wscript.exe or mses.exe
id: 38a7b0d4-2e1c-4f2a-9d5e-6a8f1b4c7d9e
status: experimental
description: Detects initial access through malicious Office documents that execute GRIFFON implant using wscript.exe or mses.exe, which are common indicators of FIN7's attack pattern.
references:
    - https://securelist.com/fin7-5-the-infamous-cybercrime-rig-fin7-continues-its-activities/90703/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\mses.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'Errors.txt'
            - 'error'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate scripts or applications using wscript.exe or mses.exe with Errors.txt
level: high

title: GRIFFON Implant Execution via PowerShell Obfuscation and JScript
id: 5b8c9d7a-1f4e-3a6b-2c8d-9e0f1a2b3c4d
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of GRIFFON implant using PowerShell command line obfuscation and JScript execution patterns consistent with FIN7's TTPs.
references:
    - https://securelist.com/fin7-5-the-infamous-cybercrime-rig-fin7-continues-its-activities/90703/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.007
    - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell.exe -NoP -NonI -ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
            - 'wscript.exe'
            - 'Errors.txt'
    condition: all of selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate PowerShell scripts using similar obfuscation
level: high

title: GRIFFON Implant Persistence via Registry Run Keys
id: 9f1e2d3c-4b5a-6c7d-8e9f-0a1b2c3d4e5f
status: experimental
description: Detects persistence mechanisms used by GRIFFON implant through registry modifications using specific task names like byzNne10.exe, c9FGG10.exe, and zEsb10.exe.
references:
    - https://securelist.com/fin7-5-the-infamous-cybercrime-rig-fin7-continues-its-activities/90703/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
    category: registry_set
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains: \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\
        Details|contains:
            - 'byzNne10.exe'
            - 'c9FGG10.exe'
            - 'zEsb10.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate software using registry run keys
level: high

id: 5a6b8c9d-1e2f-4a3b-5c6d-7e8f9a0b1c2d
status: experimental
description: Detects the exploitation of a path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) in SysAid Tomcat web service to upload a WAR archive containing a WebShell into the webroot directory, which is a key indicator of initial access.
references:
    - https://www.sysaid.com/blog/service-desk/on-premise-software-security-vulnerability-notification

    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1203
    - attack.t1189

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains|all:
            - 'usersfiles.war'
            - '\webapps\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate deployment of WAR files to Tomcat webroot
level: high

title: PowerShell Execution with Hidden Flags for Cobalt Strike Download
id: 9c8b7a6f-5e4d-3c2b-1a0f-9e8d7c6b5a4f
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell execution with -nop and -w hidden flags used to download and execute Cobalt Strike agent from a remote C2 server, indicating command and control activity.
references:
    - https://www.sysaid.com/blog/service-desk/on-premise-software-security-vulnerability-notification
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059.001/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
        CommandLine|contains|all:
            - '-nop'
            - '-w hidden'
            - 'IEX ((new-object net.webclient).downloadstring('
            - 'http://179.60.150[.]34:80/a'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using PowerShell with similar flags
level: high

The malware used techniques such as WMI for remote execution, steganography for payload embedding, and dynamic domain generation for C2 communication. Additional tools like Raindrop were used for lateral movement and deploying Cobalt Strike payloads.

pipeline.attack_summary: DarkGate malware is distributed via phishing emails containing hyperlinks that lead to MSI installers or VBS scripts. These initial payloads download and execute AutoIt-based droppers which then unpack and decrypt the final DarkGate payload using XOR encryption with base64-encoded strings. The malware communicates with C2 servers over HTTP on ports 80 and 7891, uses mutexes for process control, and implements various evasion techniques including anti-analysis checks and rootkit functionality.

Initial analysis quickly revealed significant similarity to the DarkGate malware, based on the use of a similar initial infection routine (AutoIt scripts) and the observed C2 communication protocol, which matched past analyses of the same malware family.
The AutoIt script is bundled with the .au3 file extension which is usually used for plain-text scripts. Instead it contains a pre-compiled script, which would typically use the .a3x extension.

For this infection chain, the initial payload is self-contained, meaning that all further payloads are embedded into the file and that no further payloads need to be pulled from external sources to complete the DarkGate infection. Specifically, the file contains an AutoIt executable and a corresponding script which is executed by the installer.

The script will spawn a cmd.exe shell using ShellExecute and use the curl binary that is shipped by default in current Windows installations to download an AutoIt executable and a corresponding AutoIt script.

pipeline.attack_summary: Attackers distribute Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS) via 'cracked' apps or by tricking users into pasting malicious commands into the macOS Terminal. The malware uses domain rotation to evade detection, installs persistence via LaunchDaemons, collects browser data, crypto wallets, and system files, then exfiltrates them over HTTP/HTTPS.

indicators.context: Trend™ Research analyzed a campaign distributing Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS), a malware family targeting macOS users.

Attackers disguise the malware as "cracked" versions of legitimate apps, luring users into installation. AMOS also relies on rotating domains to evade static, URL-based detections and to delay takedowns.
Trend Micro already detects this as Trojan.MacOS.Amos.PFH.

title: Initial Access via CVE-2020-0688 Exchange Deserialization
id: 1a3d7b4c-5e6f-4a9b-b2d1-0e4f6a8c2e1d
status: experimental
description: |
    This rule detects the initial access phase of CVE-2020-0688 exploitation by identifying a crafted POST request to /owa/auth.owa with valid credentials,
    followed by GET requests to ECP endpoints such as /ecp/default.aspx containing a malicious __VIEWSTATE parameter.
    The attack uses authenticated low privilege to exploit deserialization vulnerability in Exchange Server.
references:
    - https://www.trustedsec.com/blog/detecting-cve-20200688-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-on-microsoft-exchange-server/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.t1203
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_1:
        cs-method: 'POST'
        cs-uri-stem: '/owa/auth.owa'
    selection_2:
        cs-method: 'GET'
        cs-uri-stem: '/ecp/default.aspx'
        cs-uri-query|contains: '__VIEWSTATE='
    condition: selection_1 or selection_2
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using valid credentials to access Exchange ECP
level: high

status: experimental
description: Detects credential access activities using Veeam-specific PowerShell scripts that attempt to dump stored credentials.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-16
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

The text emphasizes the use of single-use URLs and messaging apps for delivery, with clear references to browser exploits and malware installation. While post-exploitation behavior is described in detail, the primary attack vector is well-defined as network-based user interaction.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with a user opening a malicious link sent via WhatsApp, which delivers a browser exploit targeting CVE-2021-31979 or CVE-2021-33771 to gain initial access and escalate privileges. The malware, DevilsTongue, uses COM hijacking for persistence, dropping encrypted DLLs and config files in system directories, and employs a sophisticated evasion technique involving stack manipulation to load legitimate DLLs while maintaining stealth. It steals credentials from browsers and Signal, and can send messages as the victim.

pipeline.attack_summary: Raspberry Robin is a worm that initially spread through infected USB drives containing LNK files disguised as folders. It uses autorun features or manual execution to launch malicious code, leveraging living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like msiexec.exe, rundll32.exe, and regsvr32.exe for execution and persistence. The malware can deploy additional payloads such as FakeUpdates, IcedID, Bumblebee, and TrueBot, leading to follow-on activities including ransomware deployment by groups like DEV-0243 (EvilCorp) and DEV-0950 (FIN11/TA505). It also disables Windows Defender's removable drive scanning feature to avoid detection.

PowerShell execution detection relies on generic '-exec bypass' and '-w 1 -enc' patterns that may trigger on legitimate administrative scripts. Consider enriching with more specific IoCs or command-line patterns.

Local administrator account creation detection uses generic 'net user admin*/add' and 'net localgroup Administrators admin /add'. These may be too broad and could miss variations in naming or command structure.
Rule for mimikatz detection uses exact filename match. This is appropriate but should be noted as potentially missing renamed variants.
WMI and RemCom detection use exact filenames, which is acceptable for known tools but may miss obfuscated or renamed versions.
